claim: Genetic alterations that activate protein kinase A (PKA) are found in many tumor types.
source: Genetic alterations that activate protein kinase A (PKA) are found in many tumor types.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by the subsequent detailed analysis of TCGA data and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: PRKACA amplification occurs at a frequency of 0.3–11.3% across multiple cancers.
source: We found a frequency of PRKACA amplification of 0.3–11.3% and a rate of activating mutations of 0.2–2.7%.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of TCGA Pan Cancer Atlas data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: PRKACA activating mutations occur at a rate of 0.2–2.7% across multiple cancers.
source: We found a frequency of PRKACA amplification of 0.3–11.3% and a rate of activating mutations of 0.2–2.7%.
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of TCGA Pan Cancer Atlas data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: PRKAR1A inactivating mutations occur at a frequency of 0.2–5.3% across multiple cancers.
source: PRKAR1A loss of function mutations were rarer, including both inactivating mutations (0.2–5.3%) and deep deletions (0.4–4%), that were predominantly detected in adrenocortical carcinoma (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: PRKAR1A deep deletions occur at a frequency of 0.4–4% across multiple cancers.
source: PRKAR1A loss of function mutations were rarer, including both inactivating mutations (0.2–5.3%) and deep deletions (0.4–4%), that were predominantly detected in adrenocortical carcinoma (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: PRKAR1A loss of function alterations are predominantly detected in adrenocortical carcinoma.
source: PRKAR1A loss of function mutations were rarer, including both inactivating mutations (0.2–5.3%) and deep deletions (0.4–4%), that were predominantly detected in adrenocortical carcinoma (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Elevated PKA activity as a consequence of GNAS or PRKACA mutations has been reported in a variety of endocrine tumors.
source: Elevated PKA activity as a consequence of GNAS or PRKACA mutations has been reported in a variety of endocrine tumors (Salpea and Stratakis, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The PRKACA L205R mutation generates an unregulated PKAc variant found in adrenocortical and ACTH-producing pituitary tumors in patients with Cushing's syndrome.
source: A prototypical example is the PRKACA L205R mutation, which generates an unregulated PKAc variant found in adrenocortical and ACTH(Adrenocorticotropic Hormone)-producing pituitary tumors in patients with Cushing's syndrome (Cao et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Patients with germline inactivating mutations in PRKAR1A are predisposed to develop myxomas, thyroid, and gonadal tumors, referred to as Carney Complex.
source: Patients with germline inactivating mutations in PRKAR1A are predisposed to develop myxomas, thyroid, and gonadal tumors, referred to as Carney Complex (Yin et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: A DNAJB1-PRKACA gene fusion has emerged as the dominant oncogenic event in fibrolamellar carcinoma (FLC).
source: Recently, a DNAJB1-PRKACA gene fusion has emerged as the dominant oncogenic event in a rare liver cancer, fibrolamellar carcinoma (FLC; Honeyman et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The DNAJB1-PRKACA fusion is found in 79–100% of FLC cases.
source: This genetic lesion is found in 79–100% of FLC (Honeyman et al., 2014; Cornella et al., 2015), with rare cases instead bearing PRKAR1A deletion (Graham et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Rare FLC cases bear PRKAR1A deletion instead of DNAJB1-PRKACA fusion.
source: This genetic lesion is found in 79–100% of FLC (Honeyman et al., 2014; Cornella et al., 2015), with rare cases instead bearing PRKAR1A deletion (Graham et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: DNAJB1-PRKACA fusions have been described in very small subsets of hepatocellular carcinoma.
source: DNAJB1-PRKACA fusions have also been described in very small subsets of hepatocellular carcinoma (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2017), cholangiocarcinoma (Nakamura et al., 2015), and oncocytic biliary tumors (Singhi et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: DNAJB1-PRKACA fusions have been described in very small subsets of cholangiocarcinoma.
source: DNAJB1-PRKACA fusions have also been described in very small subsets of hepatocellular carcinoma (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2017), cholangiocarcinoma (Nakamura et al., 2015), and oncocytic biliary tumors (Singhi et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: DNAJB1-PRKACA fusions have been described in very small subsets of oncocytic biliary tumors.
source: DNAJB1-PRKACA fusions have also been described in very small subsets of hepatocellular carcinoma (Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network, 2017), cholangiocarcinoma (Nakamura et al., 2015), and oncocytic biliary tumors (Singhi et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The PKA holoenzyme is composed of two catalytic (C) and two regulatory (R) subunits.
source: The PKA holoenzyme is composed of two catalytic (C) and two regulatory (R) subunits (Taylor et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PKA structure, supported by citation.

claim: In the inactive state, R subunits form a homodimer that binds and inhibits the C subunits.
source: In the inactive state, R subunits form a homodimer that binds and inhibits the C subunits.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PKA regulation.

claim: cAMP is generated by GPCR/Gαs-mediated stimulation of adenylyl cyclase.
source: cAMP is generated by GPCR/Gαs-mediated stimulation of adenylyl cyclase.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cAMP signaling.

claim: cAMP binding to R subunits causes a conformational change that allows greater mobility and activity of the C subunits.
source: This diffusible second messenger binds R subunits, causing a conformational change that allows greater mobility and activity of the C subunits, while maintaining localization of active kinase complexes (Smith et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PKA activation, supported by citation.

claim: A-kinase anchoring proteins (AKAPs) provide spatiotemporal specificity in cAMP signaling.
source: The spatiotemporal specificity in cAMP signaling is provided by A-kinase anchoring proteins (AKAPs).
evidence: This is established knowledge about AKAP function.

claim: The AKAP family consists of 60 human proteins that sequester PKA at subcellular locations.
source: This family of 60 human proteins sequester PKA at subcellular locations, creating nanodomains for relay and modulation of local cAMP signals (Langeberg and Scott, 2015; Omar and Scott, 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge about AKAPs, supported by citations.

claim: DNAJ-PKAc stimulates ERK activation in an FLC model system.
source: For example, DNAJ-PKAc stimulates ERK activation in an FLC model system (Turnham et al., 2019), operating via its interaction with AKAP-Lbc (Smith et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: DNAJ-PKAc operates via its interaction with AKAP-Lbc to stimulate ERK activation.
source: For example, DNAJ-PKAc stimulates ERK activation in an FLC model system (Turnham et al., 2019), operating via its interaction with AKAP-Lbc (Smith et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In GNAS-mutant pancreatic tumor cells, PKA-mediated suppression of the salt-inducible kinases (SIK1-3) supports tumor growth.
source: In GNAS-mutant pancreatic tumor cells, PKA-mediated suppression of the salt-inducible kinases (SIK1-3) supports tumor growth (Patra et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: PKA has been connected to control of the G2/M transition.
source: PKA has also been connected to control of the G2/M transition (Grieco et al., 1996; Kotani et al., 1998) and cell survival under glucose starvation (Palorini et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PKA has been connected to cell survival under glucose starvation.
source: PKA has also been connected to control of the G2/M transition (Grieco et al., 1996; Kotani et al., 1998) and cell survival under glucose starvation (Palorini et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: PKA has context-specific tumor suppressive functions including modulation of the Hedgehog and Hippo signaling pathways.
source: Interestingly, PKA also has context-specific tumor suppressive functions including modulation of the Hedgehog and Hippo signaling pathways and is mutationally inactivated in a subset of cancers (Iglesias-Bartolome et al., 2015; Tokita et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PKA is mutationally inactivated in a subset of cancers.
source: Interestingly, PKA also has context-specific tumor suppressive functions including modulation of the Hedgehog and Hippo signaling pathways and is mutationally inactivated in a subset of cancers (Iglesias-Bartolome et al., 2015; Tokita et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PKA is challenging to target directly with small molecules.
source: Despite its oncogenic action in multiple tumor types, PKA is challenging to target directly with small molecules.
evidence: This is supported by the discussion of PKA's ubiquitous role and subsequent citations.

claim: The ubiquitous role of PKAc in normal physiology makes global inhibition of the kinase a challenge.
source: The ubiquitous role of PKAc in normal physiology makes global inhibition of the kinase a challenge and selective inhibitors of this kinase have intolerable side effects (Wang et al., 2022; Toyota et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Selective inhibitors of PKAc have intolerable side effects.
source: The ubiquitous role of PKAc in normal physiology makes global inhibition of the kinase a challenge and selective inhibitors of this kinase have intolerable side effects (Wang et al., 2022; Toyota et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: FLC is a disease of young adults with only limited reported impact of chemotherapy, immunotherapy, or targeted therapy to date.
source: This challenge is particularly unfortunate in the context of FLC, a disease of young adults with only limited reported impact of chemotherapy, immunotherapy, or targeted therapy to date (Dinh et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Phosphorylation levels of the PKA target VASP pS239 increased with PRKACA induction in 639V cells.
source: Using the engineered 639V cell lines, we showed that phosphorylation levels of the PKA target VASP pS239 increased with PRKACA induction and decreased with PRKAR1AG325D induction in our global phosphoproteomics analysis (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by phosphoproteomics data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Phosphorylation levels of the PKA target VASP pS239 decreased with PRKAR1AG325D induction in 639V cells.
source: Using the engineered 639V cell lines, we showed that phosphorylation levels of the PKA target VASP pS239 increased with PRKACA induction and decreased with PRKAR1AG325D induction in our global phosphoproteomics analysis (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by phosphoproteomics data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: PKAc was upregulated with both Phosfate and MIBs platforms following dox treatment of PRKACA-inducible cells.
source: Similarly, we detected upregulation of PKAc with both Phosfate and MIBs platforms following dox treatment of PRKACA-inducible cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Phosfate and MIBs data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: YES, LYN, EPHB4, LIMK1, LIMK2, CDK5, and CDK7 kinase activities were reduced following PKAc overexpression.
source: This analysis showed that YES, LYN, EPHB4, LIMK1, LIMK2, CDK5, and CDK7 kinase activities were reduced following PKAc overexpression and increased following PKA inhibition by PRKAR1AG325D induction.
evidence: This claim is supported by integrated proteomics data analysis.

claim: YES, LYN, EPHB4, LIMK1, LIMK2, CDK5, and CDK7 kinase activities increased following PKA inhibition by PRKAR1AG325D induction.
source: This analysis showed that YES, LYN, EPHB4, LIMK1, LIMK2, CDK5, and CDK7 kinase activities were reduced following PKAc overexpression and increased following PKA inhibition by PRKAR1AG325D induction.
evidence: This claim is supported by integrated proteomics data analysis.

claim: ROCK1 was upregulated by PRKACA induction.
source: We also saw that ROCK1 was upregulated by PRKACA and downregulated by PRKAR1AG325D induction.
evidence: This claim is supported by integrated proteomics data analysis.

claim: ROCK1 was downregulated by PRKAR1AG325D induction.
source: We also saw that ROCK1 was upregulated by PRKACA and downregulated by PRKAR1AG325D induction.
evidence: This claim is supported by integrated proteomics data analysis.

claim: The pro-proliferative kinases AURKA, BRAF, and AKT2 are upregulated by PKA.
source: We focused on credentialed drug targets among the list of candidates: we observed upregulation of the pro-proliferative kinases AURKA, BRAF, and AKT2 by PKA (Figure 2C, yellow).
evidence: This claim is supported by Phosfate data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The tumor suppressor STK11 was downregulated by PKA.
source: Interestingly, the tumor suppressor STK11 was downregulated by PKA.
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomics data analysis.

claim: Network propagation analysis defined two PKA-dependent clusters with both networks including potential drug targets.
source: This analysis defined two PKA-dependent clusters with both networks including potential drug targets.
evidence: This claim is supported by network analysis of proteomics data.

claim: One PKA-dependent cluster is characterized by growth factor signaling effectors such as BRAF, multiple MAPKs, AKT, PKCs, and ERBB2.
source: One cluster is characterized by growth factor signaling effectors such as BRAF, multiple MAPKs, AKT, PKCs, and ERBB2.
evidence: This claim is supported by network analysis of proteomics data.

claim: A second PKA-dependent network includes cell cycle kinases involved in the regulation of G2/M including AURKA, PLK1, GSK3A/B, and several casein kinase family members.
source: A second network emerged, with cell cycle kinases involved in the regulation of G2/M including AURKA, PLK1, GSK3A/B, and several casein kinase family members.
evidence: This claim is supported by network analysis of proteomics data.

claim: AURKA has been previously described as a PKA target.
source: Importantly, both AURKA (Walter et al., 2000) and GSK3 (Gregory et al., 2003) have been previously described as PKA targets and can regulate MYC family proteins (Dauch et al., 2016; Gustafson et al., 2014; Gregory et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: GSK3 has been previously described as a PKA target.
source: Importantly, both AURKA (Walter et al., 2000) and GSK3 (Gregory et al., 2003) have been previously described as PKA targets and can regulate MYC family proteins (Dauch et al., 2016; Gustafson et al., 2014; Gregory et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: AURKA can regulate MYC family proteins.
source: Importantly, both AURKA (Walter et al., 2000) and GSK3 (Gregory et al., 2003) have been previously described as PKA targets and can regulate MYC family proteins (Dauch et al., 2016; Gustafson et al., 2014; Gregory et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: GSK3 can regulate MYC family proteins.
source: Importantly, both AURKA (Walter et al., 2000) and GSK3 (Gregory et al., 2003) have been previously described as PKA targets and can regulate MYC family proteins (Dauch et al., 2016; Gustafson et al., 2014; Gregory et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: FSK/IBMX treatment led to strong activation of MAPK1/3 in Colo741.
source: We observed strong activation of MAPK1/3 by FSK/IBMX in Colo741 and mild reduction in FLX1.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: FSK/IBMX treatment led to mild reduction of MAPK1/3 in FLX1.
source: We observed strong activation of MAPK1/3 by FSK/IBMX in Colo741 and mild reduction in FLX1.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: FSK/IBMX treatment led to marked inhibition of GSK3B marked by phosphorylation of its inhibitory site serine 9 in FLX1.
source: Marked inhibition of GSK3B marked by phosphorylation of its inhibitory site serine 9 in FLX1, with a smaller, transient effect in Colo741 (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: FSK/IBMX treatment led to a smaller, transient inhibition of GSK3B in Colo741.
source: Marked inhibition of GSK3B marked by phosphorylation of its inhibitory site serine 9 in FLX1, with a smaller, transient effect in Colo741 (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: FSK/IBMX treatment led to rapid phosphorylation of PKA substrates that correlated with progressive increase in c-MYC protein levels in FLX1 and Colo741.
source: Cells were treated with FSK/IBMX for 0.5, 2, or 4 hr, leading to rapid phosphorylation of PKA substrates that correlated with progressive increase in c-MYC protein levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Relatively low levels of n-MYC were detected in FLX1 but did increase with FSK/IBMX treatment.
source: Relatively low levels of n-MYC were detected in FLX1 but did increase as well (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Sustained PKAc activation resulted in mildly elevated MYC mRNA levels in FLX1.
source: Interestingly, sustained PKAc activation also resulted in mildly elevated MYC mRNA levels in FLX1 but not in Colo741 cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Sustained PKAc activation did not result in elevated MYC mRNA levels in Colo741 cells.
source: Interestingly, sustained PKAc activation also resulted in mildly elevated MYC mRNA levels in FLX1 but not in Colo741 cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Dox induction of 3xFLAG-PRKAR1AG325D in FLX1 produced reductions in PKA substrate phosphorylation and c-MYC and n-MYC levels.
source: Additionally, we generated an FLX1 cell line with dox-inducible 3xFLAG-PRKAR1AG325D, which produced the expected reductions in PKA substrate phosphorylation and c-MYC and n-MYC levels (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The engineered FLC clone had increased basal PKA activation compared to AML12 wild type.
source: Immunoblot analysis confirmed that the engineered FLC clone had increased basal PKA activation, as well as higher c-MYC expression (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The engineered FLC clone had higher c-MYC expression compared to AML12 wild type.
source: Immunoblot analysis confirmed that the engineered FLC clone had increased basal PKA activation, as well as higher c-MYC expression (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Treating FLX1 with the PKA inhibiting tool compound H89 reduced c-MYC levels.
source: In an additional control, treating FLX1 with the PKA inhibiting tool compound H89 also reduced c-MYC levels (Figure 3E).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Expression of the DNAJ-PKAc fusion protein correlated with increased protein levels of both c-MYC and n-MYC in human FLC specimens.
source: Importantly, expression of this oncogenic PKAc form correlated with increased protein levels of both c-MYC and n-MYC (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data from human FLC specimens shown in Figure 3F.

claim: MYC Targets V1 and V2 gene sets are upregulated in adrenocortical carcinoma tumors with PKA-activating alleles compared to those without.
source: The higher rate of PKA-activating alleles in adrenal cancers allowed a more robust comparison, identifying multiple upregulated Hallmark Gene Sets, including MYC Targets V1 and V2.
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: MYC Targets V2 was the only significantly upregulated gene set in ovarian cancer dataset comparing tumors with PKA activation to those without.
source: In the ovarian cancer dataset, MYC Targets V2 was in fact the only significantly upregulated gene set (Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: PRKACA knockdown caused a dramatic alteration in the FLX1 transcriptome, resulting in downregulation of Hallmark MYC Targets gene sets.
source: These caused a dramatic alteration in the FLX1 transcriptome, resulting in downregulation of Hallmark MYC Targets gene sets and upregulation of inflammatory and tumor suppressive gene sets (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNASeq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: PRKACA knockdown caused upregulation of inflammatory and tumor suppressive gene sets in FLX1.
source: These caused a dramatic alteration in the FLX1 transcriptome, resulting in downregulation of Hallmark MYC Targets gene sets and upregulation of inflammatory and tumor suppressive gene sets (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNASeq data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Both PRKACA and MYC knockdown support the expression of the canonical c-MYC transcriptional target ornithine decarboxylase (ODC) in FLX1.
source: Using individual siRNA, we knocked down PRKACA and MYC, confirming that both genes support the expression of the canonical c-MYC transcriptional target ornithine decarboxylase (ODC; Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Treatment with FSK/IBMX caused a time-dependent increase in ODC and CCND1 mRNA in FLX1.
source: Similarly, treatment with FSK/IBMX caused a time-dependent increase in ODC and CCND1 mRNA in FLX1 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Knockdown of MYC with four pooled siRNAs suppressed proliferation in FLX1 cells.
source: Knockdown of MYC with four pooled siRNAs suppressed proliferation in FLX1 cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell proliferation data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: MYC siRNA knockdown reduced proliferation in Colo741 cells, although to a lesser extent than in FLX1.
source: MYC siRNA knockdown also reduced proliferation in Colo741 cells, although to a lesser extent than in FLX1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell proliferation data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Silencing MYC leads to a significant decrease in proliferation vs. NTC in FLX1.
source: AUC analysis of growth curves is shown, demonstrating that silencing MYC leads to a significant decrease in proliferation vs. NTC; PRKACA knockdown is shown for comparison (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by AUC analysis of growth curves shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Ectopic expression of MYC using a dox-inducible system increased proliferation of FLX1 cells.
source: Conversely, ectopic expression of MYC using a dox-inducible system increased proliferation of FLX1 cells (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell proliferation data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Several Aurora kinase inhibitors were particularly potent in FLX1 cells in a screen of 352 advanced kinase inhibitors.
source: We found several Aurora kinase inhibitors in addition to the PKA-inhibiting tool compound H89 were particularly potent (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by kinase inhibitor screening data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Blocking PKA activity increased the potency of RTK, RAS/MAPK, and Aurora Kinase inhibitors in FLX1 cells.
source: These experiments revealed that blocking PKA activity increased the potency of RTK, RAS/MAPK, and Aurora Kinase inhibitors, while PI 3-kinase/mTOR pathway inhibitor effects were diminished (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by drug screening data with PRKAR1AG325D induction shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Blocking PKA activity diminished PI 3-kinase/mTOR pathway inhibitor effects in FLX1 cells.
source: These experiments revealed that blocking PKA activity increased the potency of RTK, RAS/MAPK, and Aurora Kinase inhibitors, while PI 3-kinase/mTOR pathway inhibitor effects were diminished (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by drug screening data with PRKAR1AG325D induction shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The conformation-disrupting AURKA inhibitor (CD-AURKAi) CD532 had the strongest effect on cell viability in FLX1 and Colo741.
source: We noted that the conformation-disrupting AURKA inhibitor (CD-AURKAi) CD532 had the strongest effect on cell viability.
evidence: This claim is supported by drug sensitivity data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: CD532 inhibits AURKA catalytic activity and also alters its conformation, resulting in destabilization of c-MYC and n-MYC.
source: This agent inhibits AURKA catalytic activity and also alters its conformation, resulting in destabilization of c-MYC and n-MYC (Dauch et al., 2016; Gustafson et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The partial CD-AURKAi MLN-8237 (alisertib) showed some effect in Colo-741, albeit not in FLX1.
source: Increasing our interest in this class of AURKA inhibitors, the partial CD-AURKAi MLN-8237 (alisertib) showed some effect in Colo-741, albeit not in FLX1 (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by drug sensitivity data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CX6258 and SGI1776 can each reduce c-MYC protein levels in FLX1.
source: We found that CX6258 and SGI1776 can each reduce c-MYC protein levels in FLX1, although this effect is overwhelmed by chronic stimulation of cAMP production (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The effect of CX6258 and SGI1776 on c-MYC is overwhelmed by chronic stimulation of cAMP production.
source: We found that CX6258 and SGI1776 can each reduce c-MYC protein levels in FLX1, although this effect is overwhelmed by chronic stimulation of cAMP production (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Both CD532 and MLN8237 alone can reduce c-MYC expression in FLX1 and Colo741.
source: We first confirmed that both CD532 and MLN8237 alone can reduce c-MYC expression in FLX1 and Colo741.
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: CD532 has an off-target effect on PKA activity.
source: We note an off-target effect of CD532 on PKA activity, which may explain its potent effect on cell viability.
evidence: This is inferred from western blot data showing reduced PKA substrate phosphorylation with CD532 treatment.

claim: Treatment with only MLN8237 was able to reduce c-MYC levels in Colo741, but not FLX1.
source: Treatment with only MLN8237 was able to reduce c-MYC levels in Colo741, but not FLX1, and the PIM inhibitor CX6258 had only a mild cooperative effect with MLN8237 in reducing MYC levels in FLX1 cells (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The PIM inhibitor CX6258 had only a mild cooperative effect with MLN8237 in reducing MYC levels in FLX1 cells.
source: Treatment with only MLN8237 was able to reduce c-MYC levels in Colo741, but not FLX1, and the PIM inhibitor CX6258 had only a mild cooperative effect with MLN8237 in reducing MYC levels in FLX1 cells (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Pharmacologically blocking GSK activity with CHIR99021 significantly augmented the impact of PKAc activation with FSK/IBMX on c-MYC expression.
source: Pharmacologically blocking GSK activity with CHIR99021 significantly augmented the impact of PKAc activation with FSK/IBMX on c-MYC expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Treating FLX1 cells with the proteasome inhibitor MG132 augmented the impact of FSK/IBMX on c-MYC levels.
source: Treating FLX1 cells with the proteasome inhibitor MG132 augmented the impact of FSK/IBMX on c-MYC levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A.

claim: When PKA was inhibited with PRKAR1AG325D induction, MG132 did not rescue c-MYC levels.
source: Similarly, when PKA was inhibited with PRKAR1AG325D induction, MG132 did not rescue c-MYC levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B.

claim: FSK/IBMX treatment had no significant effect on c-MYC half-life following cycloheximide treatment.
source: Thus, we tested c-MYC levels over time following treatment with cycloheximide (CHX) with or without FSK/IBMX treatment, finding no significant effect on c-MYC half-life following FSK/IBMX treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by cycloheximide chase data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Statistically significant enrichment of proteins involved in translation initiation was observed in all phosphoproteomic datasets following PKA activation.
source: We observed statistically significant enrichment of proteins involved in translation initiation in all cases (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis of phosphoproteomic data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The eIF4F complex member eIF4B can be directly phosphorylated by PKA.
source: Our previous study showed that the eIF4F complex member eIF4B can be directly phosphorylated by PKA (Coles et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Increased eIF4B phospho-S422 was observed by western blot following FSK/IBMX treatment.
source: Consistent with this, we observed increased eIF4B phospho-S422 by western blot following FSK/IBMX treatment (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: eIF4B phosphorylation is reduced following induction of PKAR1AG325D.
source: Conversely, eIF4B phosphorylation is reduced following induction of PKAR1AG325D (Figure 6C) or pooled siRNA knockdown of PRKACA in either Colo741 or FLX1 cells (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: eIF4B phosphorylation is reduced following pooled siRNA knockdown of PRKACA in either Colo741 or FLX1 cells.
source: Conversely, eIF4B phosphorylation is reduced following induction of PKAR1AG325D (Figure 6C) or pooled siRNA knockdown of PRKACA in either Colo741 or FLX1 cells (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 6D.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.
